title: During a Traffic Stop
summary: Know exactly what officers can and cannot do when they stop your vehicle
details: When a traffic police officer stops your vehicle, there is a defined legal process they must follow. Understanding this process protects you and helps you remain calm during the interaction.
dos: Stay calm and pull over safely to the left
Keep your hands visible and be polite
Ask the officer to identify themselves — name and badge number
Request an official challan slip if you are being fined
Note the officer's name, badge number, time, and location
Show digital documents (DigiLocker) — legally valid as physical copies
Ask: 'What is the specific violation?' and note the response
donts: Do NOT pay cash without getting an official receipt/challan
Do NOT hand over original documents — digital or photocopies are sufficient
Do NOT argue or physically resist — note and escalate later
Do NOT sign a blank form or any document you haven't read
Do NOT ignore if you believe the fine is wrong — note details and contest later

myths.myth: You must always pay the fine on the spot
myths.fact: You can pay online via e-challan portal within 60-90 days
Officers cannot confiscate your personal property without a court order
Supreme Court ruling confirms DigiLocker documents are fully legally valid

title: Challan & Receipt Rights
summary: Every fine must come with an official challan. No receipt = possible misconduct.
details: An official motor vehicle challan is a legal document. Any enforcement without issuing a proper challan is potentially illegal and may constitute misconduct or corruption.
dos: Always demand an official challan/receipt before paying any fine
Check that the challan has: officer name, badge number, vehicle details, violation section, fine amount
Take a photo of the challan for your records
Verify the challan online via the state e-challan portal
Pay fines through official digital payment channels
Keep challan receipts for at least 6 months
donts: Do NOT pay cash informally without an official challan
Do NOT accept verbal assurances — get everything in writing
Do NOT pay if the challan amount doesn't match the official fine for that violation
Do NOT lose your challan — it's your legal proof of payment

myths.myth: An officer can collect cash without giving a challan
myths.fact: This is illegal. Demand a challan. Report if refused.

myths.myth: You must pay extra amounts the officer mentions
myths.fact: Fines are fixed by law. No 'processing fees' or informal amounts are legal.

title: Bribery & Misconduct
summary: Being asked for informal payment? Know your rights and how to report it.
details: Any government official asking for unofficial payment (bribe) is committing a criminal offense under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988. You have rights and safe ways to report this.
dos: Stay calm — do not panic or argue aggressively
Politely decline any request for unofficial payment
Note officer details: name, badge number, location, time
If safe, discretely record audio or note details on your phone
Request an official challan — a corrupt officer will often back down
Report to the Anti-Corruption Bureau (ACB) immediately after
Use CivicShield's Report Misuse feature to document the incident
donts: Do NOT pay the bribe if it can be avoided safely
Do NOT confront or accuse the officer loudly at the scene
Do NOT delete any notes or recordings you make
Do NOT ignore the incident — reporting protects future citizens

myths.myth: Reporting corruption is dangerous and useless
myths.fact: India has legal whistleblower protection. ACB takes complaints seriously.

myths.myth: If you pay once, it's over
myths.fact: Unreported bribery encourages repeat behavior by the same officer.

title: Right to Information (RTI)
summary: Every citizen can ask any government office for information. It's your legal right.
details: The Right to Information Act 2005 gives every citizen the right to request information from any public authority. The authority must respond within 30 days (48 hours for life/liberty matters).
dos: Write a simple application addressed to the Public Information Officer (PIO)
Pay ₹10 as application fee (BPL card holders are exempt)
Clearly state what information you need — be specific
Keep a copy of your application with acknowledgement receipt
Follow up if no response in 30 days — file First Appeal to Appellate Authority
You can ask for copies of documents, inspection of records, or work samples
donts: Do NOT share your reasons for the request — you don't have to explain why
Do NOT ask for information that affects national security or personal privacy of others
Do NOT miss the first appeal deadline (30 days from response/non-response)

myths.myth: You need a lawyer to file an RTI
myths.fact: Anyone can file RTI. No lawyer needed. Simple one-page letter.
Response mandated within 30 days. Life/liberty matters: 48 hours.

title: Consumer Rights
summary: Overcharged, received defective goods, or unfair trade practice? Fight back legally.
details: The Consumer Protection Act 2019 and the establishment of Consumer Commissions give you strong legal tools when businesses violate your consumer rights.
dos: Keep all receipts, bills, and digital transaction records
Note down the name of the product, company, date of purchase
First approach the company's customer service with written complaint
File complaint on the National Consumer Helpline (NCH): 1800-11-4000
File complaint with Consumer Commission for matters above ₹1 lakh
You can claim: refund, replacement, compensation AND cost of legal proceedings
donts: Do NOT discard packaging until you verify the product works
Do NOT settle verbally — get all resolutions in writing
Do NOT miss the 2-year limitation period for filing complaints

myths.myth: Going to consumer court takes years and costs a lot
myths.fact: Consumer courts target 90-day resolution. Filing fee is nominal (₹200-2000).

myths.myth: Only big purchases can be complained about
myths.fact: Any unfair trade practice, defective good, or deficient service is valid.

title: Women's Safety Rights
summary: Special legal protections for women in public spaces, workplace, and against harassment.
details: Multiple laws protect women from harassment, stalking, assault, and workplace discrimination. Know these rights to be empowered and to help others.
dos: Report any harassment to the nearest police station immediately
File Zero FIR — you can file at ANY police station, not just the one in jurisdiction
Use the Nirbhaya App or Shakti App for instant emergency alert
Workplace sexual harassment: file Internal Complaints Committee (ICC) complaint
Demand a female officer be present when being questioned
One Stop Centre (Sakhi): available in every district for comprehensive support
donts: Do NOT accept informal resolution of sexual harassment at the workplace
Do NOT be discouraged by police inaction — escalate to SP/DCP level
Do NOT delete any digital evidence (messages, call logs, screenshots)

myths.myth: Police won't register a women's safety complaint at night
myths.fact: Zero FIR and Zero Delay protocols mandate immediate response.
PoSH Act mandates ICC in every organization with 10+ employees.

title: Free Legal Aid Entitlement
summary: If you can't afford a lawyer, the government must provide you one for free.
details: The Legal Services Authorities Act 1987 guarantees free legal aid to eligible persons through NALSA and State Legal Services Authorities (SLSA). This includes free legal representation, advice, and drafting assistance.
dos: Approach the District Legal Services Authority (DLSA) in your district
Apply for legal aid if your income is below ₹3 lakh per year
SC/ST members, women, children, disabled persons, and accident victims are automatically eligible
NALSA Helpline 15100 for immediate guidance
Lok Adalat settlements are fast, free, and binding
donts: Do NOT assume free lawyers are low quality — DLSA empanels experienced advocates
Do NOT pay anything for NALSA/DLSA provided legal services
Do NOT miss court dates provided by your legal aid lawyer

myths.myth: Free legal aid means no proper lawyer
myths.fact: NALSA empanels qualified advocates. Services are equivalent to private lawyers.

myths.myth: Only very poor people can get free legal aid
myths.fact: Women, children, SC/ST, disabled, and accident victims are eligible regardless of income.

title: FIR & Police Complaint Rights
summary: Every citizen has the right to file an FIR. Refusal by police is a criminal offense.
details: Under Section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), police are obligated to register an FIR for all cognizable offenses. Refusal to register is a punishable offense.
dos: Go to the nearest police station and request to file an FIR
If refused, send written complaint to the SP/DCP of the district
You can file complaint directly to Magistrate under Section 156(3) CrPC
Request a copy of the FIR — you are legally entitled to one free of charge
Note the FIR number — use it for all future follow-ups
Zero FIR: file at ANY police station, it will be transferred to correct jurisdiction
donts: Do NOT accept a 'Daily Diary' entry instead of an FIR for serious offenses
Do NOT let police delay your complaint without a cognizable reason
Do NOT give up if first station refuses — escalate to SP/Magistrate

myths.myth: Police can refuse to file an FIR if they feel it isn't worth it
myths.fact: Refusal to register FIR for cognizable offenses is punishable under CrPC.

myths.myth: You need to file FIR only in the area where crime happened
myths.fact: Zero FIR allows filing at any station for immediate action.
